concepts.name: Open-Ended vs Closed-Ended Mutual Funds: Structure and Liquidity
key_dimensions: Open-ended funds allow continuous entry/exit at NAV; closed-ended funds have fixed maturity and fixed unit capital
Closed-ended funds are mandatorily listed on stock exchanges for liquidity — UPSC trap: listing ≠ open-ended redeemability
Interval funds as a hybrid — redemption only during specified intervals, not continuously
NFO (New Fund Offer) period: both types launch via NFO but post-NFO behavior differs fundamentally

concepts.name: Net Asset Value (NAV): Calculation, Frequency and Misconceptions
key_dimensions: NAV = (Assets − Liabilities) / Number of outstanding units — not the same as market price for closed-ended funds
SEBI mandates daily NAV declaration for most funds; liquid funds declare NAV for every business day including previous day
NAV is NOT the performance metric alone — Total Returns Index (TRI) benchmark is the correct comparison
UPSC trap: Higher NAV ≠ expensive fund; lower NAV ≠ cheaper/better entry point

concepts.name: Equity Mutual Funds: Sub-categories and SEBI Categorization (2017)
key_dimensions: SEBI's 2017 circular mandated one scheme per category — Large Cap (top 100), Mid Cap (101–250), Small Cap (251 onwards) by market cap
Multi-cap funds must invest minimum 25% each in large, mid, and small cap — introduced after SEBI's 2020 amendment to prevent large-cap bias
Flexi-cap funds (introduced 2020) have no minimum allocation constraint across market caps — distinct from multi-cap
ELSS (Equity Linked Savings Scheme): 3-year lock-in, tax deduction under Section 80C — only mutual fund category with tax benefit

concepts.name: Debt Mutual Funds: Categories Based on Duration and Credit Risk
key_dimensions: Classification by Macaulay Duration: Overnight, Liquid, Ultra Short, Low Duration, Short Duration, Medium, Long Duration funds
Credit Risk Funds: minimum 65% in below AA-rated instruments — high yield but high default risk
Gilt Funds invest only in government securities — zero credit risk but high interest rate (duration) risk
UPSC trap: Liquid funds invest in instruments with maturity up to 91 days; NOT the same as savings accounts despite similar usage

concepts.name: Hybrid Mutual Funds: Balanced, Aggressive, Conservative and Arbitrage
key_dimensions: Aggressive Hybrid: 65–80% equity, 20–35% debt — taxed as equity fund (>65% equity threshold)
Conservative Hybrid: 10–25% equity, 75–90% debt — taxed as debt fund
Balanced Advantage / Dynamic Asset Allocation Funds: no fixed equity-debt ratio, managed dynamically using models
Arbitrage Funds: exploit price differential between cash and futures markets; taxed as equity funds despite low risk — UPSC trap on taxation

concepts.name: Index Funds vs Actively Managed Funds: Passive Investing Concept
key_dimensions: Index funds replicate benchmark (Nifty 50, Sensex) passively — lower expense ratio, no fund manager discretion
Tracking error: deviation of fund returns from index returns — key performance metric for index funds
SEBI allows only one index fund per index per AMC — limits proliferation
Active vs passive debate: In efficient markets, passive outperforms due to lower costs — relevance for pension fund investment policy

concepts.name: Exchange Traded Funds (ETFs): Structure, Trading and Government Use
key_dimensions: ETFs trade on stock exchange like shares at real-time prices — unlike mutual funds priced at end-of-day NAV
Government of India used ETFs (CPSE ETF, Bharat 22 ETF) for PSU disinvestment — a key UPSC current affairs link
Gold ETFs: backed by physical gold, each unit = 1 gram; alternative to physical gold without storage risk
Creation/Redemption mechanism via Authorized Participants (APs) — maintains ETF price close to NAV; distinct from open-ended fund redemption

concepts.name: Liquid Funds and Overnight Funds: Safety, Regulation and RBI Linkage
key_dimensions: Overnight funds invest in securities with 1-day maturity (reverse repos, overnight instruments) — lowest risk category
SEBI post-Franklin Templeton crisis (2020) tightened liquidity norms: liquid funds must hold 20% in liquid assets
Liquid funds exit load for redemption within 7 days — graded exit load introduced to prevent sudden redemptions
Used by corporates for treasury management — connects to monetary policy transmission and call money market

concepts.name: Fund of Funds (FoF): Domestic and International
key_dimensions: FoF invests in units of other mutual funds, not directly in securities — additional layer of expense ratio
International FoFs provide Indian investors exposure to foreign markets — subject to RBI's Liberalized Remittance Scheme (LRS) limits indirectly
SEBI suspended fresh inflows into international FoFs when industry crossed $7 billion overseas investment limit — regulatory cap
Taxation: treated as debt funds regardless of underlying equity holdings — UPSC trap on taxation classification

concepts.name: Sectoral and Thematic Funds: Concentration Risk and Regulatory Definition
key_dimensions: Sectoral funds invest minimum 80% in a specific sector (Banking, IT, Pharma) — highest concentration risk
Thematic funds are broader than sectoral (e.g., 'Make in India', ESG, Infrastructure) — minimum 80% in theme
SEBI allows only one sectoral/thematic fund per theme per AMC under categorization norms
Not recommended for retail investors — suitable for sophisticated investors with sector-specific views; connects to investor suitability framework

concepts.name: Solution-Oriented Funds: Retirement and Children's Funds
key_dimensions: Retirement funds and Children's funds are SEBI-defined solution-oriented categories with mandatory 5-year lock-in or till retirement/child's majority
Not the same as NPS (National Pension System) — mutual fund retirement funds lack sovereign guarantee and tax parity
ELSS has shorter 3-year lock-in vs retirement fund's 5-year — UPSC trap on comparing lock-in periods
Returns not guaranteed — distinct from EPF/PPF which offer declared/fixed returns

concepts.name: Systematic Investment Plan (SIP), SWP and STP: Mechanisms and Misconceptions
key_dimensions: SIP is an investment method, NOT a type of fund — invests fixed amount periodically into any mutual fund scheme
Rupee Cost Averaging via SIP: buys more units when NAV is low, fewer when high — reduces timing risk
SWP (Systematic Withdrawal Plan): periodic redemption — used for retirement income planning
STP (Systematic Transfer Plan): transfers from one fund to another within same AMC — used for gradual equity entry from liquid/debt fund

concepts.name: Growth vs Dividend (IDCW) Option: SEBI Nomenclature Change and Tax Implications
key_dimensions: SEBI renamed 'Dividend' option to 'IDCW' (Income Distribution cum Capital Withdrawal) in 2021 — clarifies that dividends come from investor's own capital
IDCW is NOT guaranteed — declared at AMC's discretion from distributable surplus
Post-2020 Budget: IDCW taxed in investor's hands at applicable slab rate; growth option subject to capital gains tax
Dividend stripping: buying just before IDCW and selling after to book loss — SEBI/IT regulations to prevent this

concepts.name: Direct vs Regular Plan: Cost Structure and Distributor Ecosystem
key_dimensions: Direct plans have no distributor commission — lower expense ratio, higher NAV than regular plan of same scheme
SEBI mandated direct plans for all schemes from January 2013 — promotes investor awareness
Difference in returns compounds significantly over long term — SEBI's push for fee-only advisors (RIA — Registered Investment Advisor)
UPSC trap: Both direct and regular plans are same underlying portfolio — difference is ONLY in cost, not in fund management or securities held

concepts.name: SEBI's Mutual Fund Regulatory Framework: AMFI, Trustee, AMC Structure
key_dimensions: Three-tier structure: Sponsor → Trust (Trustee) → AMC; investor money held by Trust, managed by AMC — fiduciary separation
AMFI (Association of Mutual Funds in India): self-regulatory body, not a statutory regulator — SEBI is the statutory regulator
AMFI-registered distributors (ARN holders) — KYD (Know Your Distributor) norms parallel to KYC
UPSC trap: AMFI sets guidelines but cannot penalize — only SEBI has enforcement powers over AMCs

concepts.name: Total Expense Ratio (TER): SEBI Caps, Components and Investor Impact
key_dimensions: TER includes management fees, administrative costs, distributor commission (in regular plans) — deducted daily from NAV
SEBI revised TER slabs in 2018 (lower caps for larger AUM) — larger the fund, lower the maximum TER
Equity funds have higher TER cap than debt funds; direct plans must have lower TER than regular plans by exact commission amount
Performance fee concept: SEBI allows AMCs to charge performance-linked fees above base TER under specific conditions — recent regulatory development

concepts.name: Credit Risk and Default in Debt Mutual Funds: Franklin Templeton Crisis as Case Study
key_dimensions: Franklin Templeton wound up 6 debt schemes in April 2020 due to liquidity crisis in low-rated paper — systemic risk event
Side-pocketing: SEBI-permitted mechanism to segregate stressed/defaulted assets from main portfolio — protects existing investors
SEBI response: tightened liquidity norms, restricted investment in unlisted securities, enhanced stress testing requirements
Credit rating reliance risk: AAA-rated paper can default (IL&FS, DHFL cases) — questions over-reliance on ratings in fund mandates

concepts.name: Mutual Funds and Capital Market Development: Role in Channeling Household Savings
key_dimensions: MF AUM crossed ₹50 lakh crore (2023) — financialization of household savings away from physical assets (gold, real estate)
SIP inflows as counter-cyclical stabilizer: domestic institutional investors (DIIs via MFs) offset FII outflows — reduces market volatility
MF participation in G-secs and corporate bonds — deepens bond market, aids in monetary policy transmission
Financial inclusion angle: Mutual Fund Sahi Hai campaign, Micro SIPs (₹100), and Jan Dhan-linked investments — connects to inclusive finance

concepts.name: Taxation of Mutual Funds: Equity vs Debt, LTCG, STCG and Budget 2023–24 Changes
key_dimensions: Equity funds (>65% equity): STCG at 15% (held <1 year), LTCG at 10% above ₹1 lakh (held >1 year) — no indexation
Debt funds post-April 2023: indexation benefit removed — all gains taxed at slab rate regardless of holding period — major Budget change
Arbitrage funds taxed as equity despite low risk; FoFs taxed as debt regardless of underlying — UPSC traps
STT (Securities Transaction Tax) applicable on equity fund redemption — links mutual fund taxation to securities market regulation

concepts.name: Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs) and InvITs: Mutual Fund Adjacents
key_dimensions: REITs and InvITs are NOT mutual funds but regulated by SEBI similarly — pool investor money into real estate/infrastructure assets
Mandatory 90% distribution of net distributable cash flows — income-generating unlike growth-oriented equity MFs
Listed on exchanges like ETFs; minimum investment reduced by SEBI to increase retail participation
UPSC trap: REITs invest in completed, income-generating properties only — NOT under-construction projects; InvITs in infrastructure assets
